passage: You want the travel story? Fine, Pooja, it's Irfan and here's the awkward one. First week in the hostel town, I got a nice fruit seller to laugh by making the OK sign with my hand, thumb and finger in a ring. Big grin, big thumbs-up, the whole thing. His face closed up. A woman next to him looked away. Later a local roommate told me that in some places that ring sign is rude, and the thumb can be too. Then in another city, a shopkeeper beckoned me with a curled finger and I thought, is this a hello or a telling-off? I had no idea. Now I just smile, say "namaste" with a small nod, and watch what people around me do.

qa.q: What sign did Irfan make to the fruit seller?
qa.a: Irfan made the OK sign, with thumb and finger in a ring, along with a big thumbs-up.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when the fruit seller's face closed up?
qa.a: Irfan was probably confused and embarrassed, since the friendly sign had clearly gone wrong. The face closing and the woman looking away suggest offence, though Irfan could not be sure at the time.

qa.q: What could a traveller do when unsure about a gesture?
qa.a: Smile, say a word or use a simple greeting like a small nod with folded hands, and watch what locals do before copying a sign.

qa.q: How might the fruit seller have seen Irfan's OK sign?
qa.a: The seller may have taken it as rude, even though Irfan meant it kindly, because the meaning of that ring differs from place to place.

grounding: A young adult travelling learns the OK-sign, thumbs-up and beckoning finger carry different meanings abroad and falls back on a smile and a neutral greeting.

passage: I'm Pooja, and Irfan and I were on the coach to the coast when he tried to thank the driver with a thumbs-up and the ring sign together. The driver stared, then said something short in his own language and turned back to the road. Irfan went quiet. I couldn't tell if the driver was offended or only tired, and I didn't want to guess out loud. At the next stop a woman from the tour told us that beckoning with one finger is treated as rude where she grew up. Irfan tapped his phone, looked up how people greet there, and after that he used a small smile and a nod. The driver nodded back at the end of the trip. Maybe that meant it was fine.

qa.q: Where were Irfan and Pooja travelling?
qa.a: They were on a coach to the coast.

qa.q: What might Irfan have been feeling when the driver turned back to the road?
qa.a: Irfan was probably embarrassed and unsure, which fits the sudden quiet. Pooja notes the driver might only have been tired, so the reaction is not proof of offence.

qa.q: What small step helped Irfan afterwards?
qa.a: Irfan looked up how people greet there and switched to a small smile and nod, a neutral gesture unlikely to offend.

qa.q: Why might the driver react differently from someone back home?
qa.a: In some countries the thumbs-up, ring sign or one-finger beckon can be rude, so the driver may have read them very differently from how Irfan meant them.

grounding: An observer watches a young traveller's gestures misfire across cultures and sees a smile and a nod work as a neutral greeting.

passage:
First evening in São Paulo. Ganga made a circle with her thumb and finger to tell the waiter the food was perfect. His smile froze for half a second before he moved on. Ishita, across the table, raised her eyebrows but said nothing.
Next morning Ganga asked the hostel receptionist, trying not to sound silly. The receptionist winced kindly. "For many people here that sign is rude. Young people might just laugh, but my grandmother would be shocked." Ganga covered her face, cheeks hot.
Four days later, at a fruit market, a vendor handed her a mango slice to taste. Ganga's hand started to lift into the circle, then stopped. She smiled, put a palm to her chest and said, "Obrigada, delicious!" The vendor beamed. Ishita nudged her. "Learning fast."

qa.q: What did Ganga put to her chest at the fruit market?
qa.a: She put a palm to her chest.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she covered her face at the hostel?
qa.a: She was embarrassed, with hot cheeks, on learning the circle sign could be rude; she may also have felt relieved that the waiter had only frozen for a moment.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Ganga at the market, and why?
qa.a: Stopping the circle sign and using a smile, a hand on her chest and a spoken thanks worked, because those carry no rude meaning there.

qa.q: What might the waiter have thought when Ganga made the circle sign?
qa.a: He may have taken it as rude, or he may have guessed she was a tourist meaning praise; his brief frozen smile leaves both possible.

grounding: Shows a young traveller finding that the OK-sign can offend abroad and switching to a smile and spoken thanks.

passage: Bidisha, before you pack your bag, listen to your Sarika Masi's story. At twenty I went on a college exchange to a small town in Greece. On my second day I missed the bus stop, so I stood by the road and held up my thumb to ask the next bus to wait. An old man on a bench scowled and muttered at me. I thought he was just a grumpy uncle. That evening my host, Eleni, laughed and then turned serious. "Some older people here take that thumb as an insult," she said. I felt my ears burn. I had been so proud of being friendly! After that, whenever I was unsure, I did what I did at home: palms together, a small nod, a smile. Nobody ever scowled at that. The old man on the bench even nodded back the next week.

qa.q: What did young Sarika hold up to ask the bus to wait?
qa.a: She held up her thumb.

qa.q: How did young Sarika feel when Eleni explained the thumb sign?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, her ears burning, because she had been proud of being friendly; she may also have felt grateful to learn it early.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Sarika greeted people?
qa.a: After Eleni's explanation, she chose palms together, a small nod and a smile whenever she was unsure, and nobody took offence.

qa.q: How might the old man on the bench have seen young Sarika's thumb?
qa.a: He may have taken the thumb as a rude sign from a stranger, which is why he scowled; later her folded hands and nod felt respectful enough that he nodded back.

grounding: Shows a young traveller discovering that a thumbs-up can be offensive in another country and turning to a neutral greeting.

passage: The last bus had gone, Vishal's phone was dead, and the hill-town station was packed with families shouting over the loudspeaker. Jaya knew about twelve words of the language. At the ticket window, the clerk listened to her halting question, tilted his head sideways twice and pointed to platform three. Jaya couldn't tell if the tilt meant yes, no or "maybe". She almost made the circle sign with her fingers to say "okay?", then remembered their host warning them it was rude here. Instead she held up the paper with the town's name, pointed at it, then at platform three, and raised her eyebrows. The clerk nodded firmly and wrote "21:40" on the paper. Jaya put her palms together and said one of her twelve words, "thank you". The clerk smiled. Vishal let out a breath.

qa.q: Which platform did the clerk point to?
qa.a: The clerk pointed to platform three.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she could not read the clerk's head tilt?
qa.a: She was unsure and probably anxious, with no phone and the last bus gone; the tilt could have meant yes, no or maybe, so she did not trust her own guess.

qa.q: What could Jaya try next time she is unsure what a gesture means abroad?
qa.a: She could do what worked here: skip risky hand signs, point to written words and use a simple spoken thanks with a neutral gesture.

qa.q: What would change if Jaya had made the circle sign at the window?
qa.a: The clerk might have felt insulted, and with the station crowded and time short, a stranded pair could have lost the one person helping them.

grounding: Shows a young traveller under pressure avoiding a hand sign that is rude locally and using writing, pointing and a neutral greeting instead.

passage: At the front desk of the Paharganj guesthouse, Anjali made the OK sign to a guest from Brazil, thumb and finger in a neat circle, meaning "your room is ready, all good." The woman's smile froze. She took her key and left without a word. Yamini, who had backpacked across three continents before joining the desk, winced. "In some countries that circle is a rude sign," she said softly. "A thumbs-up can offend in some places too, and so can beckoning with one finger." Anjali's face went hot. "So what do I do with my hands? We have forty guests from twelve countries this week." "Smile, say it in words, or join your palms. A namaste rarely offends anyone." That evening Anjali found the guest in the courtyard. "I think my hand said something rude this morning. I only meant everything was fine." The woman laughed with relief. "Ah! Okay. Thank you for telling me."

qa.q: What did Anjali mean by the OK sign?
qa.a: That the guest's room was ready and all was good.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel when Yamini explained the circle sign?
qa.a: Anjali felt embarrassed, her face going hot, and a little overwhelmed about what her hands might say to forty guests, when she had only meant to be friendly.

qa.q: What safer choices did Yamini suggest?
qa.a: A smile, saying it in words, or joining the palms in a namaste.

qa.q: How did the guest probably experience the day?
qa.a: She likely felt insulted by what looked like a rude gesture, then relieved when Anjali explained she had only meant everything was fine.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult finding that the OK sign, thumbs-up and beckoning finger mean different things across countries, and that a smile, words or a namaste are safer.
